h1: Raising beer prices without losing your regulars
title: Raising Beer Prices, Keeping Regulars | Craft Beer School
desc: How a brewpub can raise beer prices without losing regulars: size of rise, timing, which beers to move and what to tell drinkers.
teaser: Regulars notice a price rise. What they forgive depends on how much, how often and how you handle it.
standfirst: Costs rise every year and a brewpub that never moves its prices pays for it out of margin. The trick is to raise them in a way that your regulars barely register. We set out the size, the timing and the menu moves that help.
sections: Small and regular beats large and rare

A brewpub that holds a ₹350 pint for three years and then jumps to ₹420 will hear about it. A 20% rise in one go feels like a new price. A rise of ₹20 to ₹25, roughly 5 to 7%, once a year, usually passes with a few comments and no lost customers.

Do the arithmetic before you choose. If your beer cost has gone up ₹15 a pint since the last change, with labour and rent up by a similar amount, a ₹20 rise is not greed. It is getting back to where you were. Our guide to beer pricing strategy covers how to build the price up in the first place.
Know your margin per pint before and after

Put each beer on a sheet with its pour size, menu price, beer cost per pour and gross margin. Here is one line:

  • Pale ale, 400 ml, ₹360. Beer cost per pour, including losses, ₹55. Margin ₹305.
  • After a ₹20 rise: ₹380, cost ₹55, margin ₹325.

That ₹20 is 6.6% more margin per pour. If you sell 3,000 pours of that beer a month, it is ₹60,000. You could lose about 6% of those pours and still earn the same margin. In practice a small rise loses far less than that. The sheet shows how much room you have and stops panic about one complaint.

Do the same for food if you run a kitchen. A brewpub that raises beer and leaves food untouched for years ends up with a menu where the beer subsidises the plates. Regulars judge the whole bill, so look at both together.

You do not have to raise everything at once. Drinkers remember the price of the beer they order most, usually your house lager or flagship wheat. Moving that one is the most visible change.

Some brewpubs keep the flagship steady for a cycle and move the specials, the strong beers and the small pours first. Others move the flagship and hold the tasting paddle. Either way, decide on purpose. A price rise spread evenly across 12 beers is the one that gets noticed by everyone.

Good times to move prices are when the menu changes anyway: a new seasonal list, a redesign or the start of a new financial year. A rise lands softer when it arrives with something new.

Bad times are a slow month, the week after a poor review or the middle of a festival weekend when your busiest regulars are in. Never change prices without changing the printed menu and the till on the same day. A drinker charged more than the menu says is a complaint you deserve.
Tell the staff first and give them the reason

Your bar team takes the comments, not you. Brief them before the change. Give them a simple, honest line such as "malt and power costs went up this year, so we moved prices a little for the first time since last October." No apology, no long story.

Staff who understand the reason defend it calmly. Staff who are surprised by it tend to agree with the customer. Then the price feels unfair to everyone. Two minutes in the pre-shift huddle saves weeks of grumbling.

Regulars come for more than the price. They come for the beer being right every time, for being recognised and for the seat they like. If the beer quality wobbles in the same month you raise prices, they will connect the two.

So check the floor before you change the menu. Is every tap pouring at the right temperature, around 3 to 5 °C for most draught beers? Are the lines clean? Is the pour consistent? A rise on a perfect pint is accepted. A rise on a flat, warm one is resented.

Some brewpubs also hold a loyalty card or a regulars' happy hour steady through the rise. It costs little and tells your core drinkers that you noticed them. Keep it simple: one offer, clearly time limited, not a pile of discounts that undo the rise.
Watch the numbers for six weeks

After the change, track pours per beer per week against the same weeks before. Compare average spend per head and number of covers. If a beer drops sharply, look at it closely: the price may have crossed a line for that style or size. If nothing moves, you priced too cautiously and can plan next year's rise with more confidence.

Reading those numbers and setting prices across a whole menu is a core part of running a brewpub profitably. It rarely comes naturally to brewers.

Your first step: write your top five beers on a sheet with menu price, cost per pour and monthly pours. Add a column for a ₹20 rise. The answer will be clearer than you expect.
faqs: How much can a brewpub raise beer prices at once?
Small, regular rises of around 5 to 7% a year usually go down better than a large rise after several years of holding prices.
Should I tell customers why prices went up?
Brief your staff with one short, honest reason they can give if asked. A notice on every table usually draws more attention than the rise itself.
When is the best time to raise beer prices?
When the menu changes anyway, such as a new seasonal list or the start of a financial year. Avoid slow months and busy festival weekends.
